stem: A company depends on a critical COTS product from a small vendor and worries the vendor could go out of business. Which contractual protection BEST addresses this?

options.text: A source-code escrow arrangement releasing the code if the vendor fails
options.rationale: Source-code escrow lets the customer obtain and maintain the code if the vendor ceases operations or support, protecting business continuity.

options.text: A louder software startup sound
options.rationale: This has no bearing on vendor-failure risk.

options.text: A brighter application logo
options.rationale: Branding does not protect against vendor failure.

options.text: Ignoring the risk entirely
options.rationale: Ignoring a single-vendor dependency leaves the company exposed if the vendor fails.

stem: An executive claims that because a critical application was purchased from a vendor, the vendor bears all responsibility for its security. Which correction is MOST accurate?

options.text: The organization deploying the software remains accountable for the risk it introduces
options.rationale: Acquiring software does not transfer accountability; the deploying organization must still assess, harden, patch, and monitor it.

options.text: All responsibility fully transfers to the vendor on purchase
options.rationale: Purchase does not absolve the customer of securing what it deploys.

options.text: No one is responsible for acquired software
options.rationale: The customer retains accountability for its deployed software.

options.text: Only end users are responsible
options.rationale: End users are not accountable for the organization's software risk decisions.

stem: A developer argues that an open-source library must be secure because 'many eyes' can review the code. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Public visibility does not guarantee security; the project's health and known vulnerabilities must be evaluated
options.rationale: Open-source code can still harbor unreviewed vulnerabilities; maintenance activity, community, and known CVEs must be assessed rather than assumed safe.

options.text: Open source is always more secure than commercial software
options.rationale: Security depends on the specific project, not merely on being open source.

options.text: Open source never contains vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Open-source components frequently contain vulnerabilities.

options.text: 'Many eyes' guarantees all bugs are found
options.rationale: Many projects are under-reviewed; the 'many eyes' assumption is not a guarantee.

stem: Before acquiring a third-party application that will handle sensitive data, what should be done FIRST?

options.text: Assess the vendor's security posture and the software's known vulnerabilities/dependencies
options.rationale: Due diligence on the vendor and the product's security should precede acquisition to avoid importing unacceptable risk.

options.text: Deploy it directly to production immediately
options.rationale: Deploying unassessed software to production is risky and premature.

options.text: Grant it full admin access before evaluation
options.rationale: Granting broad access before assessment increases risk.

options.text: Publicly announce the purchase first
options.rationale: Announcements do not assess or reduce the software's risk.

stem: A newly acquired product ships with default admin credentials and many enabled features. Before production, what is the BEST practice?

options.text: Test and harden it — change defaults, disable unneeded features, apply least privilege
options.rationale: Acquired software should be hardened (default credentials changed, unused features disabled) and integrated with least privilege before production use.

options.text: Deploy it as-is with defaults to save time
options.rationale: Default credentials and unnecessary features are classic weaknesses.

options.text: Expose it directly to the internet untested
options.rationale: Exposing unhardened acquired software greatly increases risk.

options.text: Grant every user administrator rights
options.rationale: Broad admin rights violate least privilege.

stem: COTS software refers to which of the following?

options.text: Commercial off-the-shelf software purchased from a vendor
options.rationale: COTS is ready-made commercial software bought from a vendor rather than custom-built.

options.text: Custom software written entirely in-house
options.rationale: In-house custom software is not COTS.

options.text: A type of network cable
options.rationale: COTS is a software-acquisition term, not hardware.

options.text: A cryptographic algorithm
options.rationale: COTS is not an algorithm.

stem: When evaluating COTS software for a long-lived system, which support consideration is MOST important?

options.text: Whether the vendor will provide security patches for the software's intended lifespan
options.rationale: Software that will not receive patches becomes an unpatched liability; ongoing security support is critical for long-lived systems.

options.text: Whether the installer has a nice animation
options.rationale: Installer aesthetics are irrelevant to security support.

options.text: The color of the product box
options.rationale: Packaging color is irrelevant to patch support.

options.text: The vendor's office location decor
options.rationale: Office decor has no bearing on security patching.

stem: When acquiring a SaaS application, which model MOST directly governs how security duties are divided?

options.text: The shared responsibility model between provider and customer
options.rationale: SaaS security is shared: the provider secures the platform while the customer secures its data, access, and configuration.

options.text: The provider is responsible for absolutely everything
options.rationale: The customer retains responsibility for its data and configuration under shared responsibility.

options.text: The customer has no responsibilities at all
options.rationale: Customers retain meaningful security responsibilities in SaaS.

options.text: No one is responsible for SaaS security
options.rationale: Both parties share defined responsibilities.

stem: Which artifact BEST provides independent assurance of a SaaS vendor's security controls during due diligence?

options.text: A SOC 2 Type II report
options.rationale: A SOC 2 Type II gives independent, standardized assurance of the vendor's security control effectiveness over time.

options.text: The vendor's homepage tagline
options.rationale: A tagline provides no assurance detail.

options.text: A salesperson's verbal promise
options.rationale: Verbal assurances are not independent evidence.

options.text: The vendor's social media follower count
options.rationale: Follower count does not evidence security controls.

stem: To understand what third-party components are inside an acquired product so vulnerabilities can be tracked, what is MOST useful to request from the vendor?

options.text: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
options.rationale: An SBOM lists the product's components/dependencies, enabling the customer to track and respond to component vulnerabilities.

options.text: The vendor's lunch menu
options.rationale: This provides no component information.

options.text: The vendor's holiday schedule
options.rationale: Scheduling data is irrelevant to component visibility.

options.text: A marketing slide deck
options.rationale: Marketing decks do not enumerate software dependencies.

stem: A customer wants the contractual ability to verify a critical software vendor's security controls firsthand. Which clause BEST provides this?

options.text: A right-to-audit clause
options.rationale: A right-to-audit clause grants the customer authority to assess the vendor's security controls.

options.text: A non-compete clause
options.rationale: Non-compete clauses restrict competition, not enable auditing.

options.text: A force majeure clause
options.rationale: Force majeure excuses performance during extraordinary events; it does not grant audit rights.

options.text: An arbitration clause
options.rationale: Arbitration governs dispute resolution, not the right to audit.

stem: Before rolling out newly acquired software organization-wide, where should it FIRST be evaluated?

options.text: In an isolated test environment to assess security and behavior
options.rationale: Testing acquired software in an isolated environment first reveals issues before it can affect production.

options.text: Directly in production during peak hours
options.rationale: Deploying untested software to production risks outages and security incidents.

options.text: On the CEO's personal device only
options.rationale: A single personal device is not a proper evaluation environment.

options.text: Nowhere; skip evaluation to move faster
options.rationale: Skipping evaluation invites deploying vulnerable software.

stem: Beyond vulnerabilities, which additional risk is MOST important to evaluate when adopting open-source components?

options.text: License terms and compliance obligations
options.rationale: Open-source licenses impose obligations (e.g., copyleft) that can create legal/compliance risk if ignored, in addition to security concerns.

options.text: The font of the project's README
options.rationale: README formatting is irrelevant to adoption risk.

options.text: The color of the project logo
options.rationale: Logo color has no bearing on legal or security risk.

options.text: The maintainers' favorite editor
options.rationale: Editor preferences are irrelevant to adoption risk.

stem: When outsourcing custom software development, which vendor consideration is MOST important for security?

options.text: The maturity of the vendor's secure development lifecycle and code-quality practices
options.rationale: The security of delivered custom software depends heavily on the vendor's secure-SDLC and quality practices.

options.text: The vendor's office square footage
options.rationale: Office size does not determine code security.

options.text: The vendor's parking availability
options.rationale: Parking is irrelevant to software security.

options.text: The vendor's coffee brand
options.rationale: Coffee choice has no bearing on secure development.

stem: After deploying acquired software, which ongoing responsibility MOST clearly remains with the organization?

options.text: Patching and monitoring the software like any other component
options.rationale: The organization must keep acquired software patched and monitored; acquisition does not remove ongoing operational security duties.

options.text: Nothing further is ever required after install
options.rationale: Acquired software still needs patching, monitoring, and maintenance.

options.text: Deleting all logs to reduce noise
options.rationale: Removing logs harms monitoring and detection.

options.text: Assuming the vendor silently fixes everything on your systems
options.rationale: Vendors issue patches, but applying and monitoring them is the customer's responsibility.

stem: Source-code escrow primarily protects the customer in which situation?

options.text: The vendor goes out of business or stops supporting the product
options.rationale: Escrow releases the source to the customer if the vendor fails or ceases support, preserving the customer's ability to maintain the software.

options.text: The customer forgets their password
options.rationale: Escrow is about vendor failure, not password recovery.

options.text: The office loses power
options.rationale: Power loss is unrelated to source-code escrow.

options.text: A user dislikes the UI
options.rationale: UI preferences are not what escrow addresses.

stem: To ensure the organization learns promptly if an acquired-software vendor is breached, which contractual term is MOST important?

options.text: A breach-notification clause with defined timelines
options.rationale: A breach-notification clause obligates the vendor to inform the customer within set timeframes, enabling timely response.

options.text: A clause specifying the vendor's dress code
options.rationale: Dress code is irrelevant to breach awareness.

options.text: A clause about the vendor's logo colors
options.rationale: Branding terms have no bearing on breach notification.

options.text: A clause banning the vendor from using computers
options.rationale: This is impractical and unrelated to notification.

stem: Why is assessing acquired COTS software for vulnerabilities MOST challenging compared with in-house code?

options.text: The customer often cannot inspect the closed source, so it relies on vendor disclosures and external testing
options.rationale: Without source access, customers depend on vendor transparency, SBOMs, and black-box testing to understand COTS risk.

options.text: COTS software is always open source and fully visible
options.rationale: Much COTS software is closed source, limiting inspection.

options.text: In-house code can never be inspected
options.rationale: In-house code is typically fully inspectable, unlike closed COTS.

options.text: COTS software has no vulnerabilities
options.rationale: COTS software can and does contain vulnerabilities.

stem: When integrating acquired software with existing systems, which principle BEST limits the impact if the software is compromised?

options.text: Grant the software only the least privilege it needs to function
options.rationale: Least-privilege integration limits what a compromised acquired component can reach, containing potential damage.

options.text: Give the software full administrative access to everything
options.rationale: Broad access maximizes blast radius if the software is compromised.

options.text: Connect it to all systems without restriction
options.rationale: Unrestricted connectivity increases exposure.

options.text: Disable all monitoring of the software
options.rationale: Removing monitoring reduces detection of compromise.

stem: Which factor is LEAST relevant when assessing the security impact of acquired software?

options.text: The vendor's company mascot
options.rationale: A company mascot has no bearing on the security risk of the software, making it least relevant.

options.text: The vendor's patch cadence and vulnerability history
options.rationale: Patch history is directly relevant to acquired-software risk.

options.text: Contractual protections like right-to-audit and escrow
options.rationale: Contractual protections materially affect acquired-software risk management.

options.text: Known vulnerabilities in the software's dependencies
options.rationale: Dependency vulnerabilities are central to assessing acquired-software risk.
